passage: At the degree college in Hajipur, elective forms were due on Monday. Kamal had spent every clear night since Class 8 on his roof with a secondhand telescope, sketching Jupiter's moons in a notebook. The astrophysics elective was right there on the list. But Rukmini, who had taken it last year, said half the class got below a B. Kamal's scholarship needed a high average. He ticked "Office Management" instead, the one everyone called a free A. "Smart," said his roommate. Kamal nodded. That night the sky was clear. He carried the telescope up to the roof, then just sat beside it without looking through, and came down early.

qa.q: Which elective did Kamal tick instead of astrophysics?
qa.a: "Office Management", the one everyone called a free A.

qa.q: Why did Kamal sit beside the telescope without looking through it?
qa.a: He may have felt a quiet sadness, having just given up the subject he loves because he feared a lower grade.

qa.q: What could Kamal have done before ticking the safe box?
qa.a: He could have asked the astrophysics teacher or Rukmini about support, or checked what average the scholarship really needs, before letting fear decide.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had also mentioned what Rukmini enjoyed about the elective?
qa.a: Kamal might have seen the chance to learn what he loves, not only the risk to his marks, and the choice might have gone the other way.

grounding: A small-town student picks an easy elective to protect his average and gives up the subject he loves.

passage: At the university in Chicago, Jamal hovered over the course list for twenty minutes. Music Composition II, the class he had dreamed of since he started writing songs on his cousin's keyboard at twelve. Or Intro to Business Communication, which his friend Bilal said was "basically an A for showing up." Jamal had a 3.9. His pre-law adviser had said, more than once, "Protect that number." He clicked Business Communication. "Good call," Bilal texted. "Your GPA is safe." Jamal sent back a thumbs-up. Then he opened his laptop's music folder, where forty-two half-finished songs sat, and closed it again without playing one.

qa.q: How many half-finished songs were in Jamal's music folder?
qa.a: Forty-two half-finished songs.

qa.q: What does Jamal closing the music folder without playing a song suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a quiet loss; he chose safety for his grades and doesn't want to face what he gave up.

qa.q: What could Jamal try so fear isn't the only one choosing?
qa.a: He could ask the music department whether he can take the class pass/fail or audit it, so he learns without risking the number.

qa.q: Why might Bilal call it 'a good call'?
qa.a: Bilal sees only the grade side and may not know how much the composition class means to Jamal.

grounding: A student in the United States picks an easy course to protect his grade average instead of the music he loves.

passage: In the academic adviser's office at the university in Kochi, Pooja's form lay on the desk. Under "Elective" she had written "Basic Accounting". Irfan, the adviser, tapped the line. "Last semester you told me marine biology was the reason you came here." Pooja kept her eyes on her sandals. "Marine Ecology has field exams on the boat. People say it's really hard. My CGPA is 9.1. If I get a C, I lose the merit list." "Is accounting something you want to learn?" "No. But it's safe." Irfan waited. Pooja thought of the tide pools she had photographed on the field trip, the tiny crabs. She didn't change the form. Walking out, she felt as if she had shut a door very quietly.

qa.q: What did Pooja write under 'Elective'?
qa.a: "Basic Accounting".

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep her eyes on her sandals?
qa.a: She likely felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, knowing she was choosing the safe course over marine biology, the reason she came.

qa.q: What could Pooja still do before the form is final?
qa.a: She could ask Irfan what support exists for Marine Ecology, or whether one lower grade really ends the merit list, and decide with facts rather than fear.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel watching Pooja leave the form unchanged?
qa.a: Irfan may feel concerned, seeing fear of a C quietly outweigh the passion Pooja described last semester.

grounding: In an adviser's office, a student picks a safe elective to protect her grade average and never tries the field she loves.

Hi Jahnavi,
Electives closed today. I picked Office Management. Yes, I know.
Before you say anything: I wanted Historical Linguistics. You know I did. I've read half that reading list for fun. But Dr Menon's course has a reputation: most people get a B, and a B would drop my GPA below 9 for the first time. The scholarship renewal only needs 8.5, so technically I'd be fine, but still.
Office Management is a guaranteed A. Everyone says so.
It's a sensible choice. It's what any smart person would do.
I've said that to myself about eleven times since lunch.
Anyway, how are your exams? Tell me something interesting, please, because I'm going to spend next semester learning how to file memos.
Akash

passage:
Okay, Nazia, since this episode is about regrets, mine is small, but it keeps coming back.
First year, I topped the intro physics course. Loved it. The professor said, 'Shreya, take Astrophysics next year.' I went home floating.
Then I looked at the grade history. People got Cs. Actual Cs. And I had this 9.4 CGPA I'd been guarding like a baby.
So I chose Environmental Awareness. Everyone knew it was an easy A. Second year, same thing. Third year, same thing.
My CGPA is 9.6 now. Great, right?
Last month I went to the observatory open night, just to see. A second-year was explaining a star cluster, stumbling a bit, so excited. And I thought, that could have been me. With a B, maybe. But me.
I never decided to be scared. It just kept choosing for me.

Dear Sangeeta Baji,
You asked which electives I finally picked. I went with Office Management and Basic Statistics. Easy A's, everyone says. My CGPA is 9.1, and I want to keep it above 9 for master's applications.
You'll ask about astrophysics. Yes, it was open. Yes, I've wanted it since I was ten and you took me to the planetarium. But the seniors say the professor is tough and half the class gets B's. One B could drop me to 8.8. I couldn't risk it.
I keep telling myself it's the smart move. But when I walked past the astrophysics lecture hall yesterday and saw the star charts on the wall, I felt as if I'd sold something I can't get back.
Is this what growing up is? Playing safe?
Hafsa

passage: Anand, you asked why I wanted a podcast episode about playing it safe. So here's mine. I'm Ritu, final year B.Com, 8.7 CGPA. In first year I had a choice: a music minor, which I've loved since I was seven, or accounting electives. Everyone said the music professor marks hard. So I picked accounting. Safe. Every semester, same choice, same reason. My grades are lovely. I'm on track for a good job. And I haven't touched my harmonium in two years, because every time I open it, I remember I chose not to try. It wasn't really the grades making the choice. It was fear. Fear that if I tried music properly and wasn't good enough, I'd lose the one thing I thought I was good at. So I never found out. That's the part that stings.

End of semester. Vidya got her A. Deepak got a B-minus and talked about octopuses all evening. Vidya looked at her grade card, then at his photos, and couldn't work out which of them had actually won.

passage:
Kavitha, you're asking whether to take the easier elective to keep your score up. Let me, your Gautam Mama, tell you what I did at nineteen.
In Pune, in second year, we could pick one elective. There was astronomy, which I'd loved since I was a boy on the terrace with a borrowed telescope. And there was business communication, which everyone said was an easy A.
I told myself it was about my scholarship. It wasn't, really. I was scared. What if I loved astronomy and wasn't good at it? My marks would drop and so would everyone's opinion of me.
I took business communication. I got my A.
Forty years later, I still have the telescope. I still wonder. That grade didn't matter to anyone after a year. The fear chose for me, and I let it.

qa.q: Which elective did young Gautam choose?
qa.a: Young Gautam chose business communication, which everyone said was an easy A.

qa.q: Why did young Gautam really choose the easy elective?
qa.a: He was afraid of loving astronomy and not being good at it, which would drop his marks and others' opinion of him.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Gautam have chosen differently?
qa.a: At the elective choice in second year, he could have taken astronomy and accepted some risk to his marks.

qa.q: How might the friends who called it an easy A have seen Gautam's choice?
qa.a: They probably saw it as a sensible, smart move, not realising fear was behind it.

grounding: The uncle's memory shows a student choosing an easy elective to protect his grades and never trying the field he loved.

passage:
The elective registration portal closed at 5 p.m., and at 4:15 it kept crashing. Ojas sat in the college cyber café with his cousin Aadhya, refreshing again and again.
Two options: “Film-making workshop: portfolio-based grading” or “Office tools: guaranteed high scores.”
Ojas had spent every holiday since Class 8 making short films on his phone.
“So, film-making, obviously?” Aadhya said.
“My CGPA is 9.2. If the portfolio's bad, I could get a C.”
“Could.”
“And then the placement cutoff…” He trailed off. The page loaded for a second. His finger hovered over film-making, then clicked office tools.
Submitted: 4:52.
“You look like you just lost something,” Aadhya said quietly.
Ojas closed the laptop. “I kept my 9.2.”

qa.q: What was Ojas's CGPA?
qa.a: His CGPA was 9.2.

qa.q: Why did Ojas click office tools instead of film-making?
qa.a: He was afraid a bad portfolio would lower his grade and hurt his placement chances, so the safe option felt necessary.

qa.q: What could Ojas try to keep his love of film alive?
qa.a: He could join a film club or make films outside class, or talk to the film teacher about how grading works before deciding next time.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see his choice?
qa.a: Aadhya sees that he gave up something he loves, saying he looks like he just lost something.

grounding: The passage shows a student under time pressure choosing the safe, easy course to protect his grades and giving up the field he loves.

passage:
Shankar had played the sitar since he was seven. At his college in Hyderabad, there was a music composition minor, and it was all he could talk about for a month.
Then he looked at the grading: original compositions, public performance, strict jury. He looked at his 9.5 GPA.
His sister Nirmala found him with two forms. “Music composition or accounting basics?”
“Accounting,” he said.
“You hate accounting.”
“It's an easy ten. Composition could drag me down. And what if I'm not as good as I think? Then what?”
“Then you'd find out, and learn.”
“Or find out I'm average.” He signed the accounting form.
That evening, he played the sitar in his room for two hours. Nirmala listened from the corridor and didn't say anything.

qa.a: He had played the sitar since he was seven.

qa.q: Why did Shankar sign the accounting form?
qa.a: He was afraid of finding out he was average and of his GPA dropping, so fear of falling short quietly made the choice.

qa.q: What could Shankar try, even after choosing accounting?
qa.a: He could keep composing, perhaps with a teacher or a college music group, so he tests his love of music without risking the grade.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel listening from the corridor?
qa.a: Nirmala probably feels sad and worried, sensing he gave up something he loves.

passage:
"You picked Business Communication?" Yamini stared at Tanvir's screen in the library.
"It's a guaranteed A. Everyone says so."
"You've talked about astrophysics since first year. The elective's finally open to our stream."
"And Professor Iyer fails a third of the class. You know what happens to my GPA if I get a C?"
"You'd have a C. In the thing you actually like."
"Placement cut-offs, Yamini. One bad grade and the shortlist drops me."
"Did you check the cut-off?"
Tanvir paused. "Not exactly."
"So you're giving up star charts for a number you haven't looked at."
"I'm not giving up. I'm being practical." He clicked Submit before she could answer and shut the laptop. "There. Done."
Yamini watched him pack up, quiet for once.

When I look back at second year, I can see the exact afternoon it happened. I am Vikas, and I had been writing tunes on a borrowed keyboard since school. The college offered a minor in music composition. I also knew the accounting minor was, as the seniors said, "free marks."
My friend Maria took composition. She came to the hostel mess humming chord progressions, half of them wrong, and she got a B minus in the first term. I remember feeling relieved it was not me.
I finished with a shining grade sheet. Nobody ever asked to see it. Maria now plays in a small band and teaches kids on weekends.
I still have the keyboard. I don't think I chose accounting. I think I chose not to find out if I was bad at music.

qa.q: What grade did Maria get in the first term of composition?
qa.a: She got a B minus in the first term.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when Maria got a B minus?
qa.a: Vikas felt relieved it was not Vikas, which shows how afraid Vikas was of falling short in the field Vikas loved.

qa.q: What went wrong in Vikas's choice, and what could have helped?
qa.a: Fear of a lower grade made the choice; Vikas could have taken one composition course, accepted a few imperfect marks and learned whether the passion was worth it.

qa.q: How might Maria see that afternoon differently from Vikas?
qa.a: For Maria the B minus was just a start on something she loved, not a threat, which is why she kept going and now plays in a band.

passage:
Adviser's note, Department of Life Sciences — Suraj
Harsha came in on Wednesday to finalise electives. He has an excellent record. For two years he has told me about the coral reefs he watches on video, and the marine biology field course was on his form with a question mark.
He crossed it out in front of me. "Too much fieldwork grading. It's unpredictable." He chose advanced statistics, which he is good at and does not care much about.
I asked what he would do if grades did not count. He laughed and said, "Marine bio, obviously." Then he went quiet.
I did not push. I have given him the name of a fourth-year student who took the field course, and set another talk for next week, before the add-drop window closes. I would like him to decide with information, not with fear.

qa.q: What did Harsha choose instead of the marine biology field course?
qa.a: He chose advanced statistics.

qa.q: Why does Harsha go quiet after answering the adviser's question?
qa.a: He seems to realise with some discomfort that he wants marine biology and is choosing statistics only because he is afraid of an unpredictable grade.

qa.q: What did the adviser do next, and why does it help?
qa.a: They gave Harsha the name of a fourth-year student who took the course and set another meeting before add-drop closes, so he can decide with real information instead of fear.

qa.q: How might the fourth-year student's view change things for Harsha?
qa.a: Hearing from someone who survived the fieldwork grading could make the course feel less risky and show what Harsha is giving up.

grounding: It shows, through an adviser's note, a student choosing a safe course to protect his grades and nearly never trying the field he loves.

passage:
12 January, Lohri night

The bonfire on the terrace is still going, and I'm writing by its light because I don't want to go down yet.
Elective registration closed at 5 pm today. I picked Business Communication. Again. Easy A, everybody says. Eshaan picked astronomy, the one with the telescope nights and the terrifying maths, and asked, "Aren't you coming? You've been talking about stars since school."
I said I couldn't risk my CGPA. 9.1 is what I have. One B and it drops, and then placements, and then... I don't even know what then. I just know I can't be the one who fell.
So now I'm the one with an easy A in a class I'll forget, and Eshaan gets the telescope. The fire's sending little sparks up. I keep watching them.

Sarita

qa.q: Why did Sarita pick the safe elective, and how does Sarita feel about it?

qa.a: Sarita could weigh what a lower grade would really cost against years of wondering, ask the astronomy teacher about maths support, or sit in on a class first.
